meta.title: Who really said "You have power over your mind - not outside events"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: The famous Marcus Aurelius line is a modern paraphrase — it appears in no standard translation of Meditations, though the Stoic idea is genuinely his.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'You have power over your mind - not outside events'?
meta.ogDescription: A modern paraphrase, not a verbatim Marcus Aurelius quote: it appears in no standard translation of Meditations, though the Stoic idea is authentically his.

answer.label: Not a verbatim Marcus Aurelius quote — a modern paraphrase
answer.sourceLine: The idea is authentically Marcus Aurelius — his Meditations repeatedly insists that we command our own judgements, not external events. But this exact English one-liner appears in no standard translation (Long, Farquharson, Hays, Hard) and in none of Wikiquote’s sourced, disputed, or misattributed sections. It is a modern, translator-less paraphrase that condenses several passages into a slogan.

source.heading: What the record shows

docMeta.dd: Modern paraphrase — not in any standard translation

source.excerpt: If thou art pained by any external thing, it is not this thing that disturbs thee, but thy own judgement about it. And it is in thy power to wipe out this judgement now.
trail: The one-liner circulates on Goodreads ↗ and countless quote sites credited simply to “Meditations,” with no translator or book/section named.
It is absent from Wikiquote’s Marcus Aurelius page ↗ — not in the sourced Meditations quotations, nor in the Disputed or Misattributed sections.
A close reading tracing the line concludes he “likely never wrote this particular line ↗,” calling it a “collage” of themes and a victim of cumulative misattribution.
The genuine articles are passages like VIII.47 ↗: it is “thy own judgement” that disturbs thee, and “it is in thy power to wipe out this judgement now.”
source.excerptNote: The closest genuine wording — <cite>Meditations</cite> VIII.47 in George Long’s public-domain 1862 translation. Compare Book IV.3, where Long renders that “tranquility is nothing else than the good ordering of the mind.” Neither reads “You have power over your mind — not outside events.”

sourceLink.text: Meditations, Book VIII (George Long translation) at the Internet Classics Archive

source.rightsNote: The ancient Greek text and pre-1931 translations (e.g. George Long, 1862) are public domain. But this exact English wording has no identifiable translator and no documented pre-1931 appearance — it is an anonymous modern paraphrase, so we assert no copyright status for it. The public-domain George Long passages quoted above are safely reproducible; the slogan itself is of uncertain provenance.

author.name: Marcus Aurelius
author.kicker: The idea is his — the wording isn't
author.heading: About the thinker
author.bio: Marcus Aurelius Antoninus was Roman emperor from 161 to 180 AD and the last of the “Five Good Emperors.” His private notebook, known as Meditations, was written in Greek during his campaigns and never intended for publication. Its recurring theme — that we govern our own opinions and judgements while external events lie outside our control — is the seed from which this popular paraphrase grew.

cite.sourceCitation: Marcus Aurelius. <cite>Meditations</cite>. Translated by George Long. London, 1862 (public domain). Nearest genuine wording at VIII.47; the popular one-liner “You have power over your mind — not outside events” matches no standard translation and is an undocumented modern paraphrase.

copyAttribution: Popularly attributed to Marcus Aurelius, Meditations — but this exact wording is a modern paraphrase that appears in no standard translation. The nearest genuine line is Meditations VIII.47.

misattribution.heading: Quotation vs. paraphrase
misattribution.intro: This is not a case of the wrong author — the Stoic thought is squarely Marcus Aurelius’. The problem is the words: a punchy modern slogan is being presented as a verbatim quotation from Meditations.

items.why: “You have power over your mind — not outside events. Realize this, and you will find strength” matches no standard translation and is absent from Wikiquote’s sourced, disputed, and misattributed sections ↗. Quote sites list it with no edition, translator, or book number.
The distinction between what we control (our judgements) and what we don’t (external events) runs throughout Meditations — e.g. VIII.47 ↗ and IV.3. On this the attribution is fair.

misattribution.truthLine: Verdict: the thought is authentically Marcus Aurelius, but the sentence is a modern paraphrase — treat it as inspired-by, not a direct quotation. The nearest genuine line is Meditations VIII.47 ↗.

context.heading: Why the paraphrase stuck
lead: Marcus Aurelius’ <cite>Meditations</cite> is aphoristic by nature, and different translators render the same Greek very differently. That looseness is fertile ground for slogans: readers distil a recurring idea into one memorable sentence, and once it circulates it acquires the authority of a direct quotation.

The genuine passages are less quotable but more precise. Marcus does not say “you have power over your mind” as a bare assertion of willpower; he argues that things themselves cannot touch the soul — disturbance comes only from our judgements about them, which we can revise at will.
detailsBody: <cite>Meditations</cite> VIII.47 (Long): “If thou art pained by any external thing, it is not this thing that disturbs thee, but thy own judgement about it. And it is in thy power to wipe out this judgement now.”
<cite>Meditations</cite> IV.3 (Long): “tranquility is nothing else than the good ordering of the mind,” reached by retiring into one’s own soul rather than to shores and mountains.
context.pull: The thought is his. The sentence is ours.
